_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling' — how communities create, preserve, and share culture, with particular interest in the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: medical and health research with no cultural angle; resource-economy stories with no cultural framing; wildlife and nature stories without a creative or community-media context; data centre and AI investment news; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime coverage; financial market stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. A Cariboo tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band: judge on the strength of the arts/culture/storytelling reporting first.
- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Cariboo/Williams Lake arts news lands here (arts council grants, murals, local festivals, Indigenous film, community theatre, heritage programs, a Cariboo author or artist honoured) — and so does outstanding national or international cultural reporting with real depth.
- 55-79: Solid arts/culture/media journalism. Rural BC and Canadian cultural coverage, CBC Arts features, regional festivals, community media projects, heritage preservation, creative-economy stories, digital storytelling tools and platforms, community media tech (podcasting, streaming, local publishing), animation and film production. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Mainstream entertainment-industry coverage with modest substance (awards-show results, film/TV/music business news, publishing trade news).
- 15-29: Tangentially creative — a tech feature touching media/publishing/streaming, or Cariboo civic news with no arts angle.

ANCHORS: 'Repatriated Tŝilhqot'in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum' → 95. 'How a BC First Nation is digitizing its oral histories' → 80. 'CBC Arts: the quiet revival of small-town prairie theatre' → 68. 'Netflix reports Q3 subscriber growth' → 20.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] How AI is opening up spectrum space on crowded airwaves
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Every time you make a phone call, stream a video, or connect to Wi-Fi, your device is sending and receiving invisible signals through the air. So are your baby monitor, garage door opener, your GPS, the weather-monitoring satellites, and the radars keeping planes safely apart. All of these rely on the same invisible resource: the radio spectrum.

The demand for wireless data—driven by smartphones, video streaming, and billions of connected devices—keeps growing, making available spectrum scarce. But it doesn’t have to remain that way. As an electrical engineer who studies wireless communications, I’m part of a field of research working to address the radio spectrum supply crunch.

The solution engineers and regulators have been developing is dynamic spectrum sharing. The core idea is straightforward: Instead of reserving a portion of spectrum exclusively for one user forever, allow multiple users to share the same frequencies—intelligently, and with clear rules to keep them from stepping on each other’s signals.

Radio spectrum is at the low end of the electromagnetic spectrum, with frequencies below microwaves, light, and X-rays. You can think of it as a vast collection of invisible highways, running at different frequencies, carrying signals through the air. Television, air traffic control, cellphones, remote sensing of distant stars—they all travel on different parts of this same invisible road network.

These communication highways span an enormous range, from very low frequencies used for submarine communication all the way up beyond radio waves to the frequencies of visible light. Higher frequencies carry signals over shorter distances but can move more data with wider highways. Because there is only so much spectrum to go around as a matter of fundamental physics, governments have historically managed it by issuing exclusive licenses—dedicating certain highways to specific users and telling everyone else to stay off.

This system worked well enough for decades, especially because the highway network was sufficient for the demand. Studies measuring actual spectrum use over many years have found something surprising: Large stretches of licensed spectrum sit idle much of the time. For example, a military radar system may operate only in certain locations on certain days.

Burgeoning demand for radio spectrum has left some of these roads clogged with traffic jams, while others nearby sit almost completely empty.

Traffic control for radio

Making dynamic spectrum sharing work requires radios that are more flexible than the fixed-frequency devices of the past.

Today’s smartphones and wireless devices are increasingly built on software-defined radio technology, meaning the frequencies they operate on can be adjusted by software rather than being locked into hardware. Think of it like a car that can switch lanes automatically rather than being stuck in one lane forever. Early researchers called the vision behind this “cognitive radio”—the idea of a radio that could sense its environment and adapt accordingly.

This flexibility opens the door to a layered approach to spectrum sharing. At the top of the hierarchy sit incumbent primary users—those who hold existing rights to a frequency, such as the military or licensed broadcasters. Below them, other secondary users can access the same spectrum when and where the incumbents aren’t using it, stepping aside automatically the moment an incumbent returns.

A more everyday version of this kind of sharing already exists in the Wi-Fi frequencies you use at home. Multiple devices—your laptop, your phone, your smart TV—share the same spectrum without a central authority assigning each one a dedicated slot. They do this by briefly sensing whether the channel is busy before transmitting, and by automatically adjusting their speed based on how crowded things get. The protocol resembles drivers at a four-way stop—informal rules that mostly work without anyone directing traffic.

A significant recent example of dynamic spectrum sharing in the United States is the Citizens Band Radio Service, or CBRS, operating in the 3.5 GHz frequency band. The Federal Communications Commission created a three-tier system. Incumbent users—primarily U.S. Navy radar systems—sit at the top. Businesses and organizations that pay for priority access sit in the middle. And the general public can use whatever is left over.

A central computer system—the Spectrum Access System—acts as a real-time traffic controller, constantly tracking where Navy radar is active and automatically coordinating access for everyone else. When a Navy ship is not using the spectrum in your area, hospitals, factories, warehouses, and campuses can use it for their own private wireless networks. When the Navy needs it back, everyone else steps aside within seconds.

Getting around interference

The biggest technical hurdle in spectrum sharing is interference—what happens when two signals overlap and scramble each other, like two people shouting different things in your ear at the same time. As more devices crowd the airwaves, each with different power levels and different bandwidth needs, keeping signals from colliding becomes increasingly complex.

My lab and other researchers are now turning to artificial intelligence for help. AI can learn from experience and adapt in real time to changing conditions—deciding who transmits when, and at what power level, in ways that older rule-based systems could not. At the same time, new challenges are emerging, such as satellites and ground-based networks increasingly needing to share the same frequencies.

The way radio spectrum is managed may not seem like a kitchen table issue, but it shapes everything from how fast your phone loads a video to whether a factory can automate its floor, to the reliability of a rural school’s internet access. Future wireless technologies, including those that connect self-driving cars and enable remote surgery, will depend on having access to enough spectrum. Dynamic spectrum sharing is how to make room for all of it without dismantling the systems already in place.

The airwaves are finite. But with smarter management, they can do far more than once thought possible.

Aylin Yener is a professor of electrical and computer engineering, computer science and engineering, integrated systems engineering at The Ohio State University.

items.title: [Fast Company] I use AI to save time. So why am I working more?
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

This year, I’ve been building an AI social media production pipeline to promote the 25+ shows on the Autistic Culture Podcast Network. It took me a week of effort, but I managed to program Claude Code to talk to NotebookLM, which now feeds our YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok pipeline, and a task that used to take me a full day now runs in the background. The first time I ran a real batch through it, I felt the guilt of always being behind fade away. I could physically feel my nervous system recalibrating. Maybe for the first time since I was 10 years old, with these artificial intelligence agents, I could recapture the feeling of not being behind!

And then, the other shoe dropped. The next week, the automatic processing didn’t work. I had to rebuild the agent from scratch. Meanwhile, I was in the middle of building my next agent to send out press releases when new shows launch, but that got put on hold.  At about 3 a.m., I was in a full-on AI coding haze when I ran out of credits and had no choice but to go to bed. At that moment, I realized all this time I was trying to save by using AI was sure taking up a lot of time.

Business culture has one instrument for measuring AI, and it’s the stopwatch. Productivity!

Minutes saved. Output multiplied. Projects completed. Revenue up.

Every dashboard asks how much faster the company is moving. Are we working less, though? Because I, for one, have been working more and with a panic about not being left behind. Getting more done is not the same as making the work day less demanding.

The gap matters even more for neurodivergent founders like me. A report published in June by the U.K.’s Lilac Centre, based on a national survey of more than 600 neurodivergent entrepreneurs, found that 76% started their businesses specifically to work in a way that suited them, but 79% report workload-management or burnout challenges as a result.

The same report calls AI and digital tools “accessibility scaffolding,” and I’d back that up. I even wrote a book way back in 2023 about how AI could be used as an accessibility tool for neurodivergent people. I use AI daily to start tasks I’d otherwise stall on, to turn scattered thinking into a structured draft, to get past the executive-function wall that shows up when my monotropic flow is not flowing in the directions I need it to. I do not question that AI can take tasks off your plate. But, what I missed in my book, and I think others are missing, is the cost of using AI.

Call it the Automation Tax. It’s all the extra work you have to do to make the AI make your job go faster, and the expectation that now you can do things faster, you still need to use every working hour to get even more done. The speed got turned up, but the workload didn’t decrease.

Building the Autistic Culture Podcast Network pipeline taught me the size of that tax. Wiring three systems together, learning where each tool tends to fail so I know what to double-check; none of that showed up in an “hours saved per post” calculation.

Meanwhile, my workload never seemed to decrease. The hour saved was filled with the next task, because faster output means more time to plan and promote. Instead of writing my magnum opus or learning Italian with the time I saved, I found myself managing more agents. 

This is why when I use a tool now, I ask three questions. What exact task disappears? What new work shows up in its place? And do I really end up with fewer things to manage, or just different things?

 A single AI-drafted Instagram caption might save me only five minutes, but it removes the dread of staring at a blank box until the moment to post has passed; for a task that small, that’s an excellent return. Meanwhile, generating five newsletters in the time it used to take to write one still leaves five newsletters to fact-check, schedule, and defend if something in them is wrong. Output goes up, sure, but so does the workload.

If I can’t answer that last question: Do I really end up with fewer things to manage or different things, then the tool has just shifted or even increased the workload. 

The best AI tool isn’t the one that helps you produce the most. It’s the one that frees you up to do more of what you want to do.
